item.title: Family Transitions When Students Leave Home for College
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Family Transitions When Students Leave Home for College

Your student isn't the only one learning to navigate this next season.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Postsecondary isn’t just a milestone for students; it’s a transition for the entire family system.
  • While they are discovering greater independence, you’re learning a new way of being there for them.
  • Supporting your emerging adult is about helping them trust themselves while knowing you’re in their corner.

When our children are little, there's a guidebook for almost everything, from helping them sleep and make friends to learning to read and handling big emotions. Then one day they're preparing for university, college, or an apprenticeship, packing up their room for residence, and heading into their first year away from home, and the guidebook disappears.

There are orientation sessions, campus tours, and academic advisors to help them adjust into student life and greater independence, but who prepares the parents, supporters, and families who love them?

While this is one of the biggest transitions of their life, it's also one of the biggest transitions for the family system. We spend so much time preparing students for this next chapter that we rarely acknowledge what it's like for the people cheering them on.

Beginning post-secondary is a big developmental transition for young people that brings incredible opportunities and also new academic, social, and emotional challenges. Students are learning how to manage a workload they've never experienced before, build new friendships, recover from setbacks, ask for help, and balance freedom with responsibility. At the same time, families are adjusting too.

Some things to expect after sending them off to post-secondary:

  • The house feels quieter. It’s not just the empty bedroom you pass by; it’s the empty chair at the dinner table, the missing routines, and the everyday conversations.
  • You will question yourself. Should I text them? Wait for them to call? Am I helping... or hovering? Did I show up for them the way they needed when they reached out? Some moments and challenges don’t come with an obvious answer.
  • You will worry from a distance. You can no longer see how they’re really doing day to day, which can leave your imagination filling in the gaps. Something that has worked for my family is video calling over phone calls.
  • You will be adjusting to a new family dynamic. Routines shift at home, siblings are adjusting, and everyone is trying to find a new normal.

As a parent of three children, I'm familiar with how at any given moment my heart can be in four places at once: with me and with each of my children, wherever they happen to be. One reframe I like to offer families is rather than thinking about an empty nest, think about this experience as bird launching. You are helping them leave believing they can soar and do great things while knowing they always have somewhere safe to land.

Navigating This New Season

While there is no single “right” way to navigate this transition, and every family's experience will be different, here are a few gentle reminders that may help you stay connected while giving everyone room to grow.

  • They need you differently: For years, your role has been to organize, remind, solve, and protect. Now, you're moving into helping them build trust in themselves that they can think things through, solve problems, and find their way. Staying connected still matters, as does giving them room to grow.
  • Communicate expectations: It's easy to focus conversations on grades, assignments, and academic performance. While they are important, they are only one part of the conversation. Talk openly about the values you hope will guide them in this next chapter, staying connected with family, making time for siblings, the responsibilities that come with greater independence, asking for help when needed, and showing kindness. These conversations remind them that success isn't defined only by what they accomplish, but also by how they live and who they are becoming.
  • Acknowledge the emotions: This transition can bring many emotions, for them and for you. It's OK to miss them, wonder if you've done enough, and feel proud, excited, worried, and heartbroken all at once. At the same time, our emotions are not theirs to carry. Give yourself permission to process those feelings with trusted people so you can continue showing up with confidence and encouragement.
  • Be in their corner: Research tells us that one of the strongest predictors of student success isn't grades, study habits, or even time management. It's belonging. Students who feel a sense of belonging are more likely to persist through challenges, ask for help, and continue even when things get hard. One of the most important gifts we can offer is the confidence that they are not alone and they matter.
  • Ask if they are looking for comfort or solutions: When they come to you with a big feeling, try asking whether they want comfort or solutions. It's amazing how many problems we try to solve for our kids when, really, they just want someone to listen. Sometimes the most helpful response is saying: “I know this feels hard,” “I believe you can get through this,” or “I'm here with you.”
  • Support without rescuing: When we immediately remove every obstacle, we also remove opportunities for confidence to grow. When we resist rescuing and instead support them through challenges, we help them see themselves as capable and resourceful people who know how to problem-solve and make decisions. Those experiences become something powerful they can draw on for years to come.
  • Practice self-care: As you support them, remember to support yourself as well. When we care for ourselves, we strengthen our ability to show up more present, regulated, and well-resourced to handle whatever comes our way.
  • Enjoy the present: There's a tendency to see every stage of life as preparation for the next. Yet it's just as important for students, and for those who love them, to savour the season they're in. Preparing for the future matters, and so does being fully present today.
  • Keep the next reunion in view: Put the next visit or holiday on the calendar early. Having a shared date to look forward to gives both of you something steady to hold onto between now and then.
article continues after advertisement

Final Thoughts

When one member of a family leaves for postsecondary, everyone experiences a transition, and the reality is that parenting an emerging adult looks different than parenting a teenager. It requires a certain level of trust that the years of conversations, encouragement, boundaries, mistakes, healthy risk-taking, and love have helped build a strong foundation.

New beginnings aren't always easy, yet this is where hope becomes a stabilizing force. It's trusting that both you and your child have the capacity to navigate whatever lies ahead. Perhaps one of the greatest gifts we can offer them is the confidence that they can meet life's opportunities and challenges with courage, resilience, and support.

item.title: Partners in Care: How Men’s Health Impacts Women’s Health
item.description:
Infertility

Partners in Care: How Men’s Health Impacts Women’s Health

When men delay routine care, the consequences often extend to their partners.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Men often delay seeking medical care, which can postpone the diagnosis and treatment of health conditions.
  • To reduce the stigma around men's health, normalize discussions about it and encourage proactive care.
  • When men delay care, there can be consequences for both partners.

Did you know that a Cleveland Clinic survey found most men say they would rather do chores, like cleaning the bathroom or mowing the lawn, than see a doctor?1 Many of my male patients tell me they avoid medical visits because they do not want to hear bad news or be confronted with health terms they don’t understand. Some say they are embarrassed or uncomfortable, or they worry they would be judged, particularly if the concern is related to sexual health or fertility. Ideally, medical staff could help men feel more comfortable talking about these concerns, but when I teach medical students and staff, many admit that even they feel awkward asking about sexual functioning and family planning with male patients, so they wait for them to bring up the topics.

Source: miniseries/Getty Images

The toll on men’s health is obvious: A delayed diagnosis often means a more serious health problem has had time to develop and may be harder to treat. Less obvious, however, is the impact that delayed diagnosis and treatment can have on a female partner, particularly when it affects fertility or family building.

  • Since women are often the primary caregivers, navigating the health needs of babies, children, elderly parents, and grandparents, as well as their own health care, they also often assume both the task of finding doctors for the men in their life and of offering emotional support.
  • If men avoiding doctors leads to a more serious diagnosis, partners are likely to be adding caregiving and cheerleading roles to their many other roles, and dealing with their stress, depression, compassion fatigue, and fears on their own.2
  • Since male-factor infertility often means a female partner must go through an uncomfortable and time-consuming IVF egg retrieval as part of the treatment, a delay in diagnosis might mean her eggs are no longer as viable as they might have been earlier, making the couple's fertility journey even more challenging.

The good news is that the men I see going through fertility treatment keep their exam appointments, often learn to give themselves or a partner necessary injections, record their basal body temperature, and follow doctor’s orders. In other words, if motivated enough, they become good patients.

Since the theme of Men's Health Month in June of this year was "Partners in Care,” here are some ways partners can help one another stay motivated to see doctors and improve their health.

First, make joint annual appointments so you both hold one another accountable. This turns the doctor’s visit into a couple’s errand rather than being associated with emergencies. One or two uneventful exams will usually reduce anticipatory anxiety.

Next, since couples tend to share health habits3, up exercise opportunities during shared time. For example, instead of disappearing into a gym, create a home improvement project for both of you involving painting, building, or cleaning.

article continues after advertisement

Start at home. Cut back on unhealthy and high-calorie snacks, have a weight loss bet, go to sleep earlier—you get the idea. Make behavioral contagion work for you and your partner.

Lastly, don’t underestimate your influence. Eighty-two percent of the men who participated in the Cleveland Clinic's Mention It survey said the main reason they wanted to stay healthy and live longer was for their partner and other family members who depend on them.

item.title: What All Therapies Get Wrong—and What They All Get Right
item.description:
Therapy

What All Therapies Get Wrong—and What They All Get Right

Every working therapy runs the same process. There's no lingua franca, though.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Therapies disagree loudly about method while quietly running the same underlying process.
  • Every therapy regulates uncertainty, but the skill that does it is unnamed and so untrained.
  • The clinician's own mind is the instrument—foggy, uncalibrated, rarely examined as one.

In one consulting room, a patient is learning to notice a distressing thought, name it, and set it down—to stop rewarding it, so that the feeling has somewhere to go—while perhaps a few doors down, another patient is being told that the troubling thought is important to pay attention to, that growth is challenging, or perhaps even that pain in some way is good, and that avoiding such thoughts is how a person stays stuck. Another therapy provider might just wonder about the presence of such thoughts, or even ask, "What if you did, and what if you didn't?" Another might give a worksheet to take home on such thoughts. Another might recommend processing right then and there. Every one of them is competent, every one working from evidence, and each could give you a reasonable account of when one of the others would be the better choice. To boot, not all schools of therapy recognize the validity of some others.

Therapies that help people exclude negative thoughts and feelings to regulate emotion may delay, or in some cases preclude, processing those experiences—learning from them, maturing through them. Therapies that press processing run the converse risk: that the pressing exceeds a tolerance threshold for the particular individual doing the processing. Between those two failure modes, the alternatives are nearly infinite, effectively, within a tightly constrained possibility space of what is considered to be therapy (Brenner, 2009).

The Beasts in the Consulting Room

No one agrees on what therapy is. We don't even agree on what it isn't! There are pockets of agreement and areas of sharp disagreement, and the schools are divided both externally and internally. One might think of the proverbial blind men and the elephant, each groping around and feeling a different part of the animal, each concluding that their own small sample was the whole. The difference with psychotherapy is no one can decide on what the elephant is, or if even it might be an 800 lb gorilla pretending to be an elephant. It's turtles all the way down.

Every group (school, training institute, professional organization, and so on) cares about patients, I am sure, and every one also has potential conflicts of interest with patient care—economic, institutional, reputational—while patient care cannot happen at all unless there are stable institutions to house it, train for it, and pay for it. The conflict is structural—it holds the practice up—which is part of why it is so hard to look at directly.

The Error Is the Grist

Something is working across all of it regardless, underneath the part everyone argues about (Wampold, 2015).

Therapy takes BS that worked, that no longer works, and learns from the friction with reality. I mean something specific by BS—call it adaptive BS: ignoring certain inconvenient realities in order to proceed. All of us run on it. Transference is an example, and so is most of what lets a person get out of bed with an unresolved life. Adaptive BS is a working approximation rather than a failure of honesty, fit for the conditions it was built in, and the conditions move.

article continues after advertisement

When it stops fitting, you get friction. The error is the grist. The mill is the rest: analyzing the error, comparing it against what you already know, considering the models you are running and where they might be revised, identifying the zero-day vulnerabilities—the flaws that haven't caused a failure yet but will—then updating carefully, within acceptable risk margins, testing the update, taking the feedback back in, and continuing until the process is considered sufficiently effective.

All therapies have to be doing something like this if they are operationally functional.

Therapy is not the only way to facilitate human development, and not the only thing that runs this loop (Friston, 2010); it is one arrangement of it, skinned within a range of cultural, intellectual, and scientific casings over time, within a larger set of bundles. Which is one answer to what the elephant is: The blind men are each running the same animal, and what they are describing is the wrapping.

Settings With No Numbers

What I keep running into is that every step of that loop has a setting on it, and not one of the settings has a number. How fast error is admitted, how much destabilization this person can absorb today as against last month, how far a model may move in a single step before the move is itself the injury, when to stop, and who decides it has become sufficiently effective and against what threshold—every one of those is a setting, made constantly, by feel, and never specified.

article continues after advertisement

Therapy does question certainty. Arguably it does nothing else. It questions certainty with great imprecision, ordinarily, and it is very user-dependent. The actual skill isn't trained or identified.

Unidentified comes before untrained. A field cannot teach a competence it has never named, which means the variation between practitioners is structural rather than a supervision gap that more supervision would close. What gets transmitted in training is the casing, because the casing is the part that has a name.

Is the Fog the Instrument?

The next problem belongs to we clinicians. The thing metering all of this—how much doubt to introduce, how fast, how far, until when—is the clinician's own mind. Countertransference, the clinician's own reactions inside the work, is the closest thing the field has to an instrument for it (Hayes et al., 2018), and it is a foggy one: partially uncalibrated under the best of current circumstances (here's a place artificial intelligence could help), and largely invisible to the person using it.

An engineering view can define functional outcomes here; the loop is describable, and the settings are, in principle, measurable. Most therapists won't be drawn to working with precision uncertainty or engineering-type models, which is a fair preference and also part of why this has stayed unnamed. This may be where machine systems turn out effective in ways many humans can't begin to be—or, more modestly, a tool for wiping away some of the clinician's own foggy countertransference.

Wiping assumes the fog is in the way. But the fog is the grist from the miller: the disturbance or perturbation of the clinician is a perceptual and sensory surface, physiological (allostatic) and psychic. If that is right, ignoring the noise, suppressing it, or dissociating it would shift the signal we want out of consciousness. There, according to enactment models, it might affect our behavior without us noticing, shifting interpersonal interactions. Of course, that would come back over time, part of the loop of relational moves. There is more going on at any given moment than attention could hope to capture in full awareness, though over time we learn to grasp the systemic patterns, flattening linear time into wisdom.

item.title: Can AI Make Us Better Thinkers?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Can AI Make Us Better Thinkers?

New research seeks to look at thinking in the age of artificial intelligence.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • New research will map brain activity while using AI to determine what helps and hinders.
  • The objective is to build new interaction approaches that enable AI to unlock our potential.
  • The study also hopes to provide insight into whether AI enhances human production rather than replacing it.
Source: Fanatic Studio / Alamy

Against a backdrop of studies that suggest artificial intelligence (AI) is rewiring our brains, making us stupider, or easing our mental load to the detriment of critical thinking, a new study is set to evaluate whether certain contextual applications can actually make us better at thinking. That was certainly the stance of one panel at Davos a couple of years ago, where a panel on education suggested that AI could pave the way for smarter thinking if we are prepared to embrace the changes needed and to mitigate the risks in how it is applied.

New USC Study on AI and Thinking Skills

A new USC research study, funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF), is set to look at the use of AI by doctors, journalists, and software engineers and consider whether using AI can strengthen creativity and critical thinking. This investigation follows previous studies, such as the one by Stadler et al. (2024), which highlights that AI use eases mental load but at the expense of our knowledge and depth of understanding, and a study from MIT (Kos’myna et al., 2025), which found that AI reduces our recall and critical thinking and our long-term acquisition of skills.

As AI becomes a more fundamental, embedded reality of our working lives, the USC study will look at how humans and AI interact to maximise creative and critical thinking. The goal is to advance current thinking on the use of AI, and consider whether there is scope to use it to enhance a person's capacity for creativity, and ultimately to design an interaction framework to enable stronger human-AI synergy.

Monitoring Brain Activity With and Without AI During Creative and Critical Thinking

The study will identify how users interact with AI interfaces, and which type of interaction is best for sparking creativity or critical thinking. They will also work to identify the alternative: which interactions are most damaging to collaboration and creativity, and should be avoided in creative fields. Participants will be asked to complete job-related tasks using AI systems alongside a control group that will do the same without AI access. Participants' brain activity will then be monitored using electroencephalography (EEG), which will help map how ideas are formed and connected during the thinking process. Different regions of the brain become active during different types of cognitive processing, which, when compared to neutral data, will help to identify signals for creativity and critical thinking.

Critical thinking is often associated with the pre-frontal cortex, and creativity triggers sudden bursts of neural activity as well as focused attention in the brain's visual regions. This brain activity will be identifiable on the EEG and will be mapped against task type and AI usage to identify when AI can be used to encourage creative or critical thinking, and when the opposite is true.

article continues after advertisement

Researcher Souti Chattopadhyay comments, “Creativity is something that’s inherently human. This project is built on the philosophy that AI can enhance people’s ability to create and think, but it cannot replace it.”

The study also hopes to provide insight into other pressing questions that surround AI usage, including whether it creates cognitive blind spots, whether it diminishes our ability to recognise fact from fiction, and whether we can adopt AI in a way that enhances human production rather than replacing it.

Launched this month, the $600,000 project will be carried out over five years and divided into two phases. The first phase will work on classification, looking to detect specific moments that expand or narrow participants' thinking, ultimately building a map of what helps and what hinders. The second phase will build on this knowledge of the patterns, barriers, and opportunities to redesign how we should optimise interactions for better creativity and critical thinking.

The study findings may lend increased understanding to the idea originally articulated at Davos, that if we can embrace AI in the right way and mitigate its negative impacts, we can unlock significant gains in education and beyond.

item.title: Will My Estranged Child Ever Reconnect With Me?
item.description:
Forgiveness

Will My Estranged Child Ever Reconnect With Me?

How to say the words an estranged child might be ready to hear.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • An effective apology includes acknowledgment for harm done, with no excuses and no demands.
  • When parents put their healing journey into heartfelt words, it can help estranged children hear them.
  • After years of estrangement, parents may still need to wait until their child is ready to re-engage.

This is the second post in this series. Click here for the previous post.

Gray divorce refers to couples aged 50 and older ending their marriage. Currently, almost 40 percent of U.S. adults divorcing are 50 or older. Many have minor and adult children.

Father in therapy session learning what to say to his estranged daughter.
Source: Nicola Barts / Pexels

Attentively eyeing Jerrod, 55, through my office suite door, Friede, my Labrador therapy dog, greeted him with her usual enthusiasm, welcoming him into the waiting area. Reaching down to scratch her head, he began. "Hi, Friede! I'm so glad to see you today. How are you?" She immediately rolled onto her back, inviting tummy scratches. Softly, chuckling, he obliged the tummy scratches. "I already feel much calmer, Friede. Thank you for your continuing support."

We exchanged knowing glances as Friede trotted into my office with him close behind. He invited her to join him on the loveseat as she snuggled next to him. He pulled her closer. "You are the best therapy dog in the world! You know that, right?"

Therapy dogs are wonderful comfort for patients.
Source: basnetsurendra / Pexels

The three of us settled into our seats. I sat silent, allowing him the time he needed to be ready to begin. He looked at me. "I'm eager and nervous to review with you what I wrote. I've tried to stay in the present, as you always tell me, but my mind keeps slipping into imagining Madeline with tears rolling down her cheeks, as her therapist reads my apology letter to her." His words caught in his throat. Tears were softly dropping into his lap. Friede turned her head upward and looked at him. "I'm OK, Friede. I'm just sad and scared."

"You and I know you've put a lot of work into your healing and that it's natural to be sad and scared. Take as long as you need right now and let me know when you feel ready for us to look at your apology letter to Madeline with my input."

He sat for several minutes, taking slow, deep breaths as we had practiced together.

"I'm ready."

"Your apology letter is outstanding, Jerrod! Remember that it can't be perfect. I only made a few adjustments to what you wrote. Your letter addressed the appropriate points in the handout about effective apologies that I gave you last session."

"Probably the most difficult to accept is that you have no control over how Madeline will react when she and her therapist read it together. I trust her therapist's assessment that Madeline is ready to hear your apology."

article continues after advertisement

"Let's read it together. Since it's your letter, would you read it out loud slowly, and I will listen?"

He began,

My dearest Madeline,

Thank you for listening to and maybe even reading my apology letter to you. I'm guessing it will be painful for you. I am so sorry to cause you more pain than I have done already.

I know that my affair with your soccer coach was the catalyst for your mom and me to divorce and that the subsequent crisis and trauma became all-consuming at the beginning of your first year of high school and the following years.

My actions betrayed all that I had taught you about the importance of having virtues like honesty, loyalty, and trustworthiness. My actions were hypocritical to what I taught you. I betrayed the values that we both hold dear.

I caused you to experience embarrassment among your friends, family, and adults whose opinions you cared about. I was focused only on myself and caused you devastating harm and pain. My actions destroyed our intact family.

During each of your high school years, I was not being the father you deserved. I was impatient with you, didn't listen to you, was closed-minded, yelled at you, threatened to take things away from you, and blamed and shamed you for not understanding me and being happy for me.

I am ashamed that I hurt you and broke your trust in me, thus breaking our daughter-father bond. I caused you to struggle all four years of high school, not sleeping, not being able to focus on your schoolwork, drowning in your hurt, disappointment, and loss.

My deep sorrow and remorse course through every part of my body and psyche.

I have spent the last six years in therapy to heal myself and become the father you deserve. I pledge to you that I will do everything I can to heal our daughter-father relationship, and I will never hurt you with such behavior as I did back then.

I will continue being here for you in every way I can. I have not and will not abandon you. I will continue to support you financially, as I have done for the last six years.

I hope you can forgive me one day, and I understand if you're not ready now."

We sat in silence for a minute or so.

"I didn't expect reading it out loud would be cathartic for me, but it was. I'm ready for you to send it to Madeline's therapist. I've done the best I know how to do."

"I agree that you have done the best you can do now, Jerrod. Now we wait."

Patient name and details changed to preserve confidentiality.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Taking the Games Out of Online Dating
item.description:
Mating

Taking the Games Out of Online Dating

Separating app design from genuine human connection.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Gamification in online dating apps tends to interfere with building connections more so than finding them.
  • Desires for both quantity and quality are primary competing goals in online dating.
  • Secure attachment can help protect against gamification on dating apps.

Have you ever felt as though you were a player in someone else’s game? When game design features are incorporated into an experience that is not normally a game, such as forming an intimate relationship, we call this “gamification.”

In many circumstances, gamification can enhance our interest and enjoyment in everyday life. For instance, say you’ve made a game out of a long car ride to pass the time, or you’ve paired an otherwise mundane task with a reward or a challenge. These strategies are generally supported when they help us engage more meaningfully with ourselves, others, and the world. With online dating, however, the use of gamification is considerably more difficult to endorse.

Source: Kirill_Savenko / iStock

Gamifying Love

While online dating apps openly use gamification features to engage their users, recent research has linked these features with dating fatigue, self-esteem concerns, overstimulation, carelessness, obsessive-compulsive behaviours, and a sense of dejection. Though it might feel tempting to write off dating apps altogether, let’s take pause and consider the nuances:

What seems to matter most is how an intimate relationship is nurtured after matching, rather than how you matched. This means that so long as games have no place in the actual development of a connection, a healthy relationship can still begin by "swiping right" on your phone. Although the popular Hinge slogan "The dating app designed to be deleted" may contradict their gamified strategies, this doesn’t automatically mean you won’t find love online.

Quality vs. Quantity

Dating apps are an ideal example of how more is not always better. With what may seem like an endless number of potential partners, men and women alike have reported feeling overwhelmed and unsure of how to trust, engage, and ultimately select who they’d prefer to date. Most notably, gamification is at play when users report a sense of compulsivity with checking their online dating notifications and statistics, including number of matches, likes, and messages. Naturally, research has shown that both a false sense of high or low self-worth can come from respectively high or low reciprocity on these platforms.

Source: grinvalds / iStock

This is where our human need for connection hits a ceiling—particularly when it comes to monogamy. In other words, a user’s desire for abundant matches might block them from establishing a healthy intimate relationship with one individual. This is the game between short-term validation and long-term romance.

article continues after advertisement

Fortunately, we have the aptitude to pause and shift out of autopilot mindfully. By extending compassion to yourself for holding competing desires, you’ll find you are one step closer to experiencing quality over quantity in romantic relationships. Ironically, and favourably, the development of an emotionally mature relationship tends to include short-term gratification and long-term investment. Especially online, romance deserves more than to be quantified, and users deserve more than to be "played."

Secure Attachment to the End Game

Secure attachment is recognized as a protective factor against the gaming features of online dating. This means feeling securely attached within yourself and witnessing secure attachment within your potential partner. Indicators of secure attachment include one’s comfort with authenticity and vulnerability, openness to different opinions, high self-esteem, confidence, and resilience, and a desire for balance between intimacy and independence.

Source: Tero Vesalainen / iStock

It intuitively follows that those who display more securely attached qualities also demonstrate more intentional and regulated dating app engagement. This has been measured in contrast to users who align with more anxious or avoidantly attached behaviours. Specifically, in a 2026 study out of Europe, anxious attachment was linked with lower self-esteem and obsessive app usage, and avoidant attachment was associated with usage for escapism and attempts to self-regulate.

article continues after advertisement

Despite common misconceptions about attachment styles, neuroscience reveals how these classifications are flexible rather than fixed personality traits. With that in mind, I invite you to take a judgment-free but honest inventory of your attachment style patterns lately—and those of your partners—before making your next move. If secure attachment feels far away right now, (1) you are not alone, (2) you hold the power to uncover secure attachment within yourself, and (3) it is not your job to fix or uncover secure attachment in a dating partner.

Above all, you deserve to feel securely attached to yourself, which means courageously choosing authenticity over immediate abundance and desire from others. You are not a player in someone else’s game, nor are your dating partners in your life story. If you wish, you deserve to use the apps without the apps using you.

item.title: How to Push Back Against Teen Nonchalance
item.description:
Adolescence

How to Push Back Against Teen Nonchalance

To counter teen nonchalance, send the message that romantic feelings matter.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Nonchalance—choosing detatchment over drama—has become a social media buzz term, especially for teens.
  • The adolescent brain isn't wired to play it cool.
  • Owning big feelings doesn't mean you'll get what you want. But it's the only way to learn how to care.

Until recently, the word nonchalance brought to mind the image of a woman walking down a street in Paris, wearing large-framed, elegant sunglasses, unbothered by the bustle of the city. She is classy, cool, and in control.

Now what I see is a teen reacting to emotional blows with studied indifference. Nonchalance has become a social media buzz term, with TikTok creators proclaiming, “I am so unbothered,” choosing peace and detachment over drama, especially when it comes to relationships.

The Adolescent Brain

What’s fascinating about this trend (which also affects single adults) is that it flies in the face of much of what we know about adolescence. The teen brain does not make it easy to play it cool. The amygdala, nucleus accumbens, and other brain regions involved in emotional reactivity and reward seeking mature faster than the prefrontal cortex, an area that helps us exercise self-control.

But in an era when any unguarded moment could end up in a viral video and an impulsively needy text could be screenshot and shared, young people have come to see detachment as the answer. Dating (a term so official that young people are reluctant even to use it) is rife with ambiguity. You might while away hours texting with someone you’re into, sensing something big building between you, only to have the person stop the exchange without explanation, leaving you and your feelings in the virtual dust. You might be sharing confidences and having sex with a partner for months, yet one or both of you refuse to call what’s happening “a relationship.” All this entails holding back in a seemingly endless game of who cares less.

In such an environment, nonchalance may seem like a refuge. You have every reason to want to be that woman on the street in Paris, even if your amygdala isn’t playing along. The tactic is not at all new. The suppression of enthusiasm or neediness evolved as an emotional regulation strategy to protect social status, maintain control, and project high mate value.

Yet, when you get young people talking openly about the idea of nonchalance, what comes clear is this: They hate it. I teach an interdisciplinary college seminar called "Love and Heartbreak." When I brought up the term in class, everyone groaned. They called BS on the trend, but were troubled over how to free themselves from it. All this, of course, flies in the face of true nonchalance. It isn’t really working if all you’re doing is concealing the storm behind the sunglasses.

So, how do we help young people push back against the pressure to be nonchalant? Relationship expert Alexandra Solomon and others have embraced the term “chalant” as a cultural pushback against the pose of dating apathy. She urges people to be brave about letting themselves feel excited and attracted—and to insist that doing so does not make them weak.

Romantic Feelings Matter

As the author of First Love: Guiding Teens Through Relationships and Heartbreak, I emphasize that parents and other supportive adults can help young people resist the pressure to play it cool by sending the message early on that romantic feelings, even if they’re not reciprocated, matter. Parents often dismiss what their children go through as “just a crush,” unreal and unimportant—while, to the young person experiencing them, the feelings are the most real thing in the world. Showing support, care, respect, and curiosity to a child with a crush won’t make the crush worse. Instead, you’re demonstrating that you value romantic feelings as an essential and meaningful part of being human.

Later, if your teen is struggling to be nonchalant in a confusing situationship, you can reframe the problem by asking: Why be ashamed of having a big heart and big feelings? Why be ashamed of wanting one of the greatest rewards of human existence—the love and attention of a devoted partner in a healthy relationship? These questions don’t mean your child will get what they want. That we have no control over. But they will help your child see that being the person who wants more is not weak, and that acknowledging how you feel is the only way to find out what is truly possible with someone else.

article continues after advertisement

If that leads to disappointment, as it very well may, you have an opportunity to remind your child that the pain of rejection is necessary and inevitable. Feeling it, naming it, and living through it is how young people build the emotional muscle they’ll need for every relationship that follows. If they keep hiding behind the sunglasses of nonchalance, they may lose the chance to practice the harder—and much more valuable—skill of actually caring.

item.title: 7 Child "Wants" That Are Really Childhood Needs
item.description:
Parenting

7 Child "Wants" That Are Really Childhood Needs

Children can't name what they need, so they show you through their behavior.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Attention-seeking behavior is almost always a bid for connection.
  • Giving children choice over how a task happens often resolves resistance without removing the boundary.
  • Children who tantrum or defy are often longing to be taken seriously, and escalate less when they are.
  • When both people's needs are visible, conflicts stop being about who wins and start being about what works.

This is Part 3 of a series.

In the first post in this series, I discussed the fact that what parents call needs are almost always strategies, one specific way of hoping a real need will get met. In the second post, I walked through seven common examples of parents' "needs” and the real needs they’re pointing to. When you can name the real need underneath, more solutions become available.

The same reframe works in the other direction. What parents dismiss as children's "wants" are almost always needs too, which children are expressing the only way they know how.

The behavior is the communication. Here are seven of the most common examples.

1. "They just want attention."

Behavior: Stalling at bedtime, clinging at school drop-off, following you from room to room

Underlying need: Connection, belonging, or being understood

One thing to try: Build a short one-on-one time routine earlier in the day, even one that lasts just 10 minutes, where your child leads the play, and your phone is away. A child whose longing for belonging is being met regularly is less likely to try to squeeze it out of every bedtime moment.

2. "They want to make everything difficult."

Behavior: Hitting, screaming, refusing to get dressed, melting down over small things

Underlying need: Comfort, autonomy, or connection

One thing to try: Look at what was happening in the environment before the behavior started. Was it loud, crowded, or physically uncomfortable? Addressing the sensory environment before the next difficult stretch often reduces the behavior without any direct intervention.

3. "They always want to have their own toys—and everyone else's too!"

Behavior: Inability or unwillingness to share

Underlying need: Respect, consideration, or connection

Sharing is a genuinely hard concept for young children who don't yet have a strong awareness of time. From their perspective, "Share!" means: "Give up the toy you're enjoying, with no clear idea of when you'll get it back." No wonder they resist.

article continues after advertisement

Toy-taking can also be a bid for play with a sibling or peer, or a bid for connection with you, if you tend to appear the moment a sibling cries.

One thing to try: Set aside a few toys that are your child's alone and designate everything else fair game. Encourage children to develop their own strategies—a timer, or finding out whether another toy could substitute. These approaches allow needs for respect and consideration to be met by the children themselves, rather than by one child simply giving in.

4. "They just want to play all the time."

Behavior: Resisting transitions away from play, ignoring requests, saying "just one more minute" repeatedly

Underlying need: Play, joy, connection, or autonomy

One thing to try: Treat their play with the same respect you would want someone to show your work. Ask when they will be done, in the context of other things you both want to do that day, rather than imposing your time limit on them.

5. "They want to control everything."

Behavior: Refusing to brush teeth, resisting getting dressed, saying no to things that seem reasonable

Underlying need: Autonomy or choice

One thing to try: Some issues really are about health and safety. In that context, try to find as much flexibility as you can within the framework of making the activity happen. Which toothbrush, which toothpaste flavor, which tooth first, which room they brush in, and potentially whether they brush twice a day or only once. A child who has some say over how something happens is often much more willing to do it.

article continues after advertisement

6. "They want to push my buttons."

Behavior: Tantrums, hitting a sibling, not stopping when asked, doing the exact thing you just said not to do

Underlying need: Respect or autonomy

One thing to try: Before redirecting the behavior, try to understand what the child was attempting to do or communicate. "What were you trying to do?" or "Why is this important to you?" A child who experiences being taken seriously tends to need to escalate far less.

7. "They want to fight about everything."

Behavior: Resisting chores, arguing back, refusing to cooperate with simple requests

Underlying need: Collaboration or ease

One thing to try: Instead of telling them to do it, ask what they would be willing to do. "I do not want the clothes to stay on the floor. What could we do to make sure that does not happen?" A child who helps come up with the solution is far more likely to follow through with it.

And if they still resist, the task may be too difficult for them. If you have a need for collaboration, work together to find a task your child is willing and able to help with. My daughter found making her lunches under time pressure on weekday mornings to be overwhelming. So I make her lunch and she unloads the dishwasher, which requires much less mental effort and meets her need for ease.

Final Thoughts

Across all three posts in this series, the pattern is the same. What parents call needs are strategies pointing to something real underneath. What children do that parents read as wants are needs too.

When you can see the need underneath the behavior, it stops being about who is right and starts being about what could work for both of you.

That's what the needs framework makes possible: a way of being in a relationship where both people's needs are held with equal care.
